newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Trade sees Chinese soymeal interest but offers low.
newsitem.headline: Trade sees Chinese soymeal interest but offers low.

text.p: Asian traders are anticipating a soymeal price war once Chinese buyers get over their National Day holiday, trading sources said on Friday.
"PRC buyers are showing interest but it is well below replacement value from the U.S.," a Singapore trader said.
"They need spot shipment, like yesterday," he said.
Chinese inquiries were targeting prices below $300 a tonne for low-protein U.S. soymeal in 50,000-tonne Panamax lots.
"Under $300 for prompt (delivery) is not available. They are trying to see if vessels and players can switch to their requirements to improve prices and interest," he said.
Minimum c&f (cost and freight) per-tonne to Far East ports was around $315 to $318 per tonne for low-protein soymeal. High/low protein was $305 to $307, traders said.
Cargoes arriving at $290 a tonne were booked two months ago, traders said. No new deals could be confirmed on Friday.

Traders throughout the Far East have told Reuters they expect China to import between one million and 1.2 million tonnes of soybean meal in 1996. They said 600,000 tonnes should have arrived at Chinese ports by mid-September.
Soymeal futures on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) were boosted on Thursday in part by rumours China was seeking 150,000 tonnes of soymeal.
CBOT soymeal futures closed US$1 per tonne higher to $4 lower, with the October contract up $1 at $247.80.
Continuing talk that U.S. soybean yields are coming in much higher than expected had forced CBOT prices down $10 to $15 a tonne in the past week, traders said.
"Sentiment is bearish," another trading source said.
"Buyers are pushing the price further. There is going to be a price war. In the next couple of days we will see the market react to this," he said.
Demand for animal feed -- of which soybean meal is a principal component -- had slowed dramatically in the first half of the year, but appeared to be picking up, sources said.
"In the first half of this year, there was lousy demand for meal," a Western industry source said. "The second half was okay and it will continue to get better," he said.
Pork prices were up to 5.20 yuan ($0.62) a lb (half kg), from 4.70 yuan in March, he said. Chinese sources concurred, saying they were paying between five and eight yuan a lb.
Day-old chick prices were up 133 percent on March's 1.20 yuan to 2.80 yuan each, the industry source said.
One Beijing source said she was paying 10.50 yuan per lb of fresh chicken, and up to 30 yuan for a whole bird. She said prices had not changed for the past three months.
"Farmers will be keen to grow more pigs and chickens," the industry source said. "Demand will be good next year."
China's October 1 National Day, the 47th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, was celebrated with a three-day public holiday.
Far East traders said they did not expect Chinese business to pick up until next week -- and then there could be a sweep on the soymeal market before prices rallied.

"They're not stupid, they can see futures are dropping," a Hong Kong trader said. "We have explained to our customers that there is not much old crop left in the U.S. and the South Americans are not willing to sell at low prices."
But, he and other traders said, it could take Chinese buyers time to react to the dips.
"They don't move fast enough," said one.

"For the Chinese, each transaction is very complicated -- they must make sure they have an end-buyer and have a credit line. Decisions are made by committee and it can take so long they miss the boat," he said.
